For every control, name the quality attribute, business effect, person checking it and correction process. Route the unanswered questions to the relevant reviewer. This practical table helps reveal mixed purposes; it is not a statutory safe harbour or a complete survey of uncontrolled-licensing case law.

practicalOutput: A control-purpose matrix and two linked records: trademark quality/use evidence and the broader operating-relationship factsheet.
limitations: Statutory distinction only. No complete licence-validity, abandonment, trademark case-law or franchise-coverage conclusion is made.

title: Why is a sanctions name search only the first step?
description: Match the actual party, trace relevant ownership and assess the proposed transaction under the right restrictions.
learningSummary: A screening tool can return a possible name match without deciding whether the person is the same party or whether the transaction is permitted. An unlisted business can also be affected through ownership rules. Keep identity, ownership and the transaction as separate questions.

keyTerms.meaning: The Consolidated Screening List, combining specified Commerce, State and Treasury lists as an aid.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control, which administers the ownership rule discussed here.
A person subject to the relevant blocking treatment; not every list entry has identical restrictions.
The OFAC ownership rule reaching entities 50% or more owned in aggregate by blocked persons, including relevant indirect ownership.

sections.heading: A similarity score is not transaction clearance
paragraphs: Commerce says apparent CSL matches need additional due diligence and confirmation against the official source list. A fuzzy-name score measures similarity, not the probability that a deal is lawful.

Record names, aliases, appropriate identifiers, addresses, source list and search date. Explain why an apparent match is or is not the actual party. Do not treat all lists alike: identify the restriction associated with the particular source and person before deciding the consequence.

sections.heading: Ownership can affect an entity not separately listed
paragraphs: OFAC FAQ 401 explains direct/indirect ownership and aggregation under the 50 Percent Rule. Its examples show why simply multiplying every percentage can mislead. If a blocked person owns 50% of Entity A, A is blocked; A’s 50% ownership of Entity B can in turn make B blocked.

A search for Entity B’s name alone could miss that result. Trace the chain and apply the actual ownership rule rather than assuming a missing name means no restriction. Equally, do not replace the prescribed analysis with an informal control test.

sections.heading: Control and other transaction restrictions remain separate
paragraphs: FAQ 398 says control without 50% aggregate ownership is not automatic blocking under this ownership rule, but warns about other designation/blocking criteria and dealings involving a blocked representative. Below 50% is therefore not universal permission.

Party screening also does not settle goods or technology, destination, end-use, country-programme or authorisation requirements. A country connection is not always a blanket ban, just as a clean name result is not a complete export decision.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a prospective distribution partner
paragraphs: A brand considers a distributor whose name produces no apparent match. The team records the result but also obtains the relevant ownership chain and the proposed goods, destination and use. It assigns any unresolved source-list and transaction questions before payment, access or shipment depends on clearance.

The screening register should identify the reviewer and source-specific result, then be revisited when parties, ownership, goods or restrictions change. This site performs no live search and does not certify a partner as clean.

practicalOutput: A screening-and-transaction register documenting identity matches, ownership, source-specific restrictions, actual transaction facts and remaining questions.
limitations: No live designation result, country/programme decision, export classification, licence or transaction authorisation is provided.

title: Can a brand require common prices across its network?
description: Distinguish brand/operator restrictions from coordination among competing businesses and review the actual policy.
learningSummary: A brand may want consistent prices, territories or customer allocations across independent operators. The competition-law analysis depends on who agrees, who competes and how the policy works. A federal case changing the standard of review did not make every network pricing policy lawful.

keyTerms.meaning: A restriction between businesses at different supply levels, such as a supplier and dealer; the actual relationships matter.
Coordination between competitors, distinct from a supplier imposing its own policy.
A legal approach treating a defined category as unlawful without the fuller analysis discussed here.
An assessment of the actual arrangement and competitive context, not automatic approval.
Minimum advertised price terms, whose actual reach needs separate examination.
Most-favoured-nation terms linking one party’s treatment to others; their conditions also require review.

sections.heading: Understand what Leegin actually decided
paragraphs: In Leegin Creative Leather Products v. PSKS,551 U.S. 877(2007), the Supreme Court majority overruled the prior Dr. Miles federal per-se treatment of vertical minimum resale-price agreements and required rule-of-reason analysis. The Court reversed and remanded—sent the case back for further proceedings.

That outcome is not a finding that every policy, or the particular arrangement, was lawful. The cited record supplies the 2007 majority’s standard and disposition, not an independently checked later merits outcome. Current FTC guidance also explains that state-law treatment can differ.

sections.heading: Map who competes and who makes the decision
paragraphs: FTC guidance distinguishes manufacturer/dealer restrictions, unilateral policy decisions and competitor coordination. A network can contain several relationships, especially where the brand also operates units.

Record whether operators coordinate or collectively pressure the brand. Calling an arrangement vertical does not settle horizontal effects. State and international minimum-price rules may also differ from the federal framework. MAP, MFN, territory and customer restrictions require their own actual terms to be examined.

sections.heading: Fictional example: operators ask for a common price
paragraphs: Several independent service operators ask the brand to establish a common network price. The brand also has its own operating unit. Rather than assuming the request is an ordinary brand standard, the team preserves who proposed it, the communications, competitive relationships and intended enforcement.

The reviewer can then distinguish suggested from required prices, unilateral decisions from agreement, and the claimed service/quality purpose from effects on competition. The example clears no price policy or customer allocation and makes no finding about the fictional parties.

sections.heading: Prepare the policy before announcing it
paragraphs: Keep the proposed rule, discounts, advertising support, territories, reserved customers and methods used to induce compliance. Preserve communications and evidence supporting any claimed service investment.

Build a policy/party/effects file with separate federal, state and international questions. The standard of review tells the reviewer what must be examined; it is not a badge of legality to place beside a standard price list.

practicalOutput: A policy/party/effects file explaining the pricing or allocation restriction, communications, competitive relationships and jurisdiction-specific questions.
limitations: No antitrust clearance, later Leegin outcome or complete case-law survey is supplied. No MAP, MFN, territory, customer or collective-pricing arrangement is approved.

title: Is your service worker an employee or an independent business?
description: Separate the codified wage interpretation, investigation policy, proposed changes and tax test before using contractor treatment.
learningSummary: A contract can call a worker independent without deciding the legal result. Different federal and state rules can ask different questions about the same arrangement. Begin with the person’s real business activity and identify which test and source status apply.

keyTerms.meaning: The Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal wage-and-hour law relevant to the interpretation discussed here.
An inquiry into the working relationship as a whole, not just the contract label.
Instructions about how an agency investigates; not necessarily a repeal or change in private legal rights.
A suggested regulatory change that is not effective merely because its comment period has ended.
Whether a court challenger is entitled to bring the case; different from deciding every underlying legal issue.

sections.heading: Understand why the source dates look inconsistent
paragraphs: In the existing November 12, 2026 review, current 29 CFR Part 795 still contains the 2024 economic-reality interpretation. It examines the whole activity with six nonexclusive factors; no single factor or chosen subset necessarily decides the result.

The Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division issued a May 1, 2025 bulletin telling investigators to use a different approach within its stated scope and discretion. It expressly says it does not change employees’ rights or employers’ responsibilities. A February 27, 2026 proposed rule seeks rescission/replacement and proposed expansion to the Family and Medical Leave Act and the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act. Those source types must not be treated as interchangeable.

rows: Codified agency interpretation of the whole relationship
Directs the stated investigation approach using 2008 Fact Sheet 13
Repeal, waiver of private rights or reopening of closed cases
An effective replacement because comments have closed

sections.heading: Collect business facts rather than scoring labels
paragraphs: Record who sets prices and schedules, accepts jobs, hires helpers, makes entrepreneurial investments, markets to other customers and bears a genuine opportunity for profit or loss. Include actual practice and reserved rights.

Under the codified interpretation, specialised skill alone does not establish an independent business. A licence, contract label or remote location does not settle status either. Do not turn a multifactor inquiry into a points tally. Explain the circumstances and missing evidence so the governing test can be applied.

sections.heading: Fictional example: the “independent” technician
paragraphs: A maintenance brand’s agreement calls a technician an independent contractor. The operations file shows mandatory schedules, brand-set prices and the technician’s equipment purchases, but says little about outside customers, hiring helpers or opportunity for profit and loss.

The team gathers those missing facts instead of announcing a result from either the label or one investment. It then identifies the current governing wage-law, tax and relevant state tests. This example classifies no worker; it shows how to produce a file useful under more than one inquiry.

sections.heading: Keep the IRS inquiry separate
paragraphs: Internal Revenue Service (IRS) employment-tax guidance groups common-law evidence into behavioural control, financial control and the type of relationship. It examines the whole relationship rather than a magic number of factors; a right to control can matter for remote workers.
A payroll-tax decision or relief provision is not a universal answer under the FLSA or state unemployment/wage law. Give each test its own authority, date, unresolved question and responsible person.

sections.heading: Read the court example within its limits
paragraphs: The January 9, 2025 Colt & Joe Trucking opinion/order found the challenger lacked standing and explained that its arguments would otherwise fail or were waived. It did not classify every driver or service technician. The February 2026 proposal reports appeals/stays as of its publication; the latest appellate dockets were not independently checked.

The bulletin and proposal also cite different associated opinion numbers; this guide does not reconcile or apply those opinions. Keep dated case reporting distinct from a current judicial-status assertion. The practical output is one worker-facts file plus a separate test/status register before relying on contractor treatment.

practicalOutput: A worker-facts file and a dated test/status register separating wage law, investigation policy, proposals, court limits and employment tax.
limitations: No worker, exemption, tax relief or state-law result is determined. Latest appellate dockets are unverified, and differing associated opinion references are not reconciled.

title: Can the brand and local operator both have employer duties?
description: Map real employment decisions and shared hours, then apply the NLRA and wage-law inquiries separately.
learningSummary: A local operator may employ the team while a brand, customer or related company also influences the work. Joint-employer analysis asks whether more than one entity has responsibilities under a particular employment law. There is no single test that answers every law—or the separate franchise-definition question.

keyTerms.meaning: An entity treated with another as an employer under the particular applicable legal test.
The National Labor Relations Act; its joint-employer inquiry differs from the federal wage-law inquiry.
The Fair Labor Standards Act, concerning federal wage-and-hour responsibilities.
A contractual right to act even if not exercised; its relevance depends on the actual test.
A court setting aside an agency rule, rather than deciding every future employment relationship.

sections.heading: The current NLRA rule was restored through final action
paragraphs: The National Labor Relations Board’s (NLRB’s) February 27, 2026 final action states that the 2023 rule never took effect after district-court vacatur and restores the 2020 text immediately. Current§ 103.40 matches that action. Substantial direct and immediate control over one or more listed essential employment terms is central; indirect or unexercised reserved authority has the rule’s qualified supplementary role.

This is the NLRA framework, not a rule for every employment statute. Do not convert its treatment of one kind of control into a general conclusion that all brand standards are safe or that a brand can never be an employer.

sections.heading: Keep the court step and the wage-law position clear
paragraphs: The Chamber of Commerce v. NLRB opinion/order was ordered March 8, 2024 and filed March 18 as Document 47. Its remedy discussion states that final judgment will vacate the 2023 replacement and removal of the earlier text. The 2026 final rule independently confirms the resulting regulatory action. The cited court document is not a complete current docket search.

For the FLSA, current Part 791 is reserved. That does not mean joint-employer liability disappeared. DOL’s April 23, 2026 publication is a proposal, not an effective rule or franchise safe harbour. Governing court law and actual employment facts remain relevant; the NLRA history does not answer them.

sections.heading: A real agency example: one worker, two businesses
paragraphs: DOL Opinion Letter FLSA2025-05 addresses a restaurant and members club with represented shared operations, managers and workers. On those supplied facts, DOL concluded the worker’s hours had to be combined and both employers were responsible for FLSA compliance.

The lesson is that separate incorporation or payroll systems did not answer that inquiry on those facts. The letter expressly limits its view to the information supplied. It is not a court judgment about every franchise or every pair of related businesses.

sections.heading: Build a control-and-hours map
paragraphs: For each entity, record who selects workers, sets pay and individual schedules, directs performance, disciplines and terminates. Keep service/brand standards and employment decisions in separate columns, including mixed-purpose controls.

For example, an inspection of the contracted service outcome and a direct instruction about a named worker’s shift should be recorded accurately rather than both labelled quality control. Neither fact alone decides the complete test. Add shared-worker hours, managers and actual practice so the reviewer can assess the NLRA, FLSA and relevant state questions separately.

sections.heading: Do not confuse this with franchise classification
paragraphs: A franchise inquiry examines the brand, operating control/assistance and payments. Joint-employer inquiries concern responsibilities for workers under their own laws. One relationship file may contain relevant facts for both, but a conclusion under one test does not establish the other. Keep each result and its limits visible in the operating plan.

practicalOutput: A control-and-hours map with distinct NLRA, FLSA, state-law and franchise-classification questions and source/status records.
limitations: No joint-employer finding, full circuit survey, bargaining-unit or state-law clearance is supplied. The 2026 FLSA proposal is not an effective franchise exemption.

title: Who handles product certificates and serious safety information?
description: Separate product scope, import certification and prompt reporting rather than treating a certificate as approval.
learningSummary: A brand importing or distributing equipment needs to know which product-safety rules apply and who performs the required tasks. A B 2 B invoice or branded label does not settle jurisdiction. Certification and reporting serious safety information are separate responsibilities.

keyTerms.meaning: The Consumer Product Safety Commission, the agency for the certificate/reporting pathway discussed here.
The identified party legally responsible for the applicable certificate’s validity, accuracy, completeness and availability.
The prescribed electronic certificate-data filing process for covered imports.
Foreign-trade zone; specified entries have a different phase date under the reviewed final action.
The evidential threshold relevant to reporting; not every complaint automatically establishes a reportable defect.

sections.heading: Identify the actual product and intended users
paragraphs: The consumer-product definition and exclusions require a factual scope check. Identify the article, ordinary users, intended use, materials and other agencies potentially involved. Neither a business customer nor an equipment label alone answers that legal question.

This guide covers the CPSC certification/reporting pathway. It does not determine an electrical, machinery, food, pesticide or workplace standard for an unidentified product. Keep those specific questions assigned rather than marking an entire import file product-safe.

sections.heading: Assign certification to a named responsible party
paragraphs: For covered imported finished products, Part 1110 defines the importer/certifier role, certificate contents and eFiling process. It permits specified broker/owner/purchaser/consignee allocations, while the identified certifier remains legally responsible for validity, accuracy, completeness and availability.

Identify the actual rules and testing basis. A bought template does not demonstrate that the product satisfies them. The part also includes five-year supporting-record requirements and conditions for access/furnishing. Give those records an owner distinct from the logistics booking contact if necessary.

sections.heading: Use the real phase dates and distinguish enforcement policy
paragraphs: The final action makes the requirements effective July 8, 2026 for most covered products. Specified FTZ entries have a January 8, 2027 phase, still future at the existing November 2026 review. Do not apply one date to every entry.

CPSC’s FAQ describes an initial policy of not seeking entry denial solely for missing eFiling data while continuing certificate enforcement. That is an enforcement description, not an exemption, guaranteed entry outcome or permission to ignore applicable safety rules. It is also time-sensitive and should not be treated as permanent grace.

sections.heading: Give complaint escalation a separate reporting route
paragraphs: Covered firms can have an immediate reporting duty when information reasonably supports the specified noncompliance, a potentially substantial product hazard or an unreasonable serious-injury/death risk (15 U.S. Code § 2064(b)). The timing rule interprets immediate as 24 hours with its weekend/holiday computation, and warns against waiting for complete risk estimates (§ 1115.14).

A reasonable investigation is not automatic permission to delay once reportable information is known. Identify who receives complaints, preserves evidence and makes prompt escalation possible. A supplier’s promise to handle the issue does not settle every other entity’s duty.

sections.heading: Fictional example: certification does not close a safety complaint
paragraphs: A brand has an import certificate file for a consumer product and later receives information about overheating. The product lead preserves the complaint and available facts and routes them for the actual reporting-threshold assessment. The earlier certificate is not used as a reason to ignore new information.

The team records the product, applicable standard, certifier, evidence and reporting owner. It does not assume a recall, reportable defect or shipment clearance from this example. Unverified tests, technical standards, fees and other authorisations stay unresolved until supported.

practicalOutput: A product/standard/certifier/record matrix linked to a complaint-to-reporting process with named owners and applicable phase dates.
limitations: No product jurisdiction, test result, approval, recall decision or shipment clearance is made. The import overview was inaccessible; cited operative rules, final action, FAQ and statutes were used. The eFiling policy does not waive certificate or safety duties.

title: When does overseas system access trigger the federal data-security rules?
description: Identify the data, people, transaction and exact thresholds before treating a remote account as permitted or prohibited.
learningSummary: A U.S. business may give overseas staff or a partner access to customer and employee systems. Data can remain on a U.S. server while the foreign user can read it. Part 202 asks a specific national-security question about defined parties, data and transactions—not whether every overseas connection is automatically forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: The rule’s broad concept including reading, viewing, editing or otherwise receiving data through systems or cloud platforms.
A person or entity within Part 202’s defined categories, not simply anyone with a foreign address.
Data exceeding the applicable category threshold under the prescribed aggregation rules.
The rule’s separately defined category with specified regardless-of-volume criteria.
A covered arrangement permitted only subject to its actual security and other conditions, distinct from a prohibition or exemption.

sections.heading: Map who can see the data, not just where it is stored
paragraphs: The first screen identifies the U.S. person, foreign/covered person, data, volume and agreement. Remote support access can matter even when no file is downloaded or the database stays in the United States. Conversely, a foreign address alone does not establish a prohibited transaction.

Part 202’s countries-of-concern and covered-person definitions have their own ownership, organisation, employment, primary-residence and designation rules. The recorded list names China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia and Venezuela, with China’s stated Hong Kong/Macau definition. Citizenship alone or an OFAC name result is not the complete test; an unlisted entity can meet a defined category.

sections.heading: Use the exact counts and aggregation period
paragraphs: Government-related data has specified regardless-of-volume criteria. Bulk U.S. sensitive personal data uses category-specific thresholds and the preceding 12 months with the specified same-party conditions. A new invoice does not reset the total.

The table preserves the rule’s “more than” comparisons and its distinction between persons and devices. Mixed datasets have their own rule and need separate assessment. These counts do not provide a safe harbour for government-related data or other privacy laws.

headers: Bulk threshold under the stated category conditions

sections.heading: Separate prohibited, restricted and exempt arrangements
paragraphs: Data brokerage and specified human-omic transactions have prohibitions. Relevant vendor, employment and investment transactions can be restricted, subject to the actual security and other conditions. Restricted transactions require the current diligence programme and annual audit conditions.

There is a bounded exemption for corporate-group administrative/ancillary operations. An ordinary independent franchise or licence partner is not assumed to be a qualifying subsidiary or affiliate. Identify the exact exemption and facts rather than treating all brand-network activity as internal. Do not replace prescribed security requirements with controls the company merely regards as equivalent.

sections.heading: Fictional example: an overseas helpdesk account
paragraphs: A U.S. operator proposes overseas helpdesk access to its system. The project team first records what the user can view or edit, which data categories and volumes are involved, the parties’ relevant status and the contract. It does not conclude that storage in the United States removes the access question.

The reviewer then assesses whether a defined transaction, prohibition, restriction or supported exemption applies. This example authorises no account. Detailed CISA technical security requirements were not read through the access-blocked resource in the existing review, so those implementation questions remain explicit.

sections.heading: Keep operative dates separate from expired enforcement policy
paragraphs: The programme took effect April 8, 2025. The operative diligence/audit provisions use October 6, 2025. The DOJ overview’s October 5 wording is a recorded source difference; the guide follows§§ 202.1001–1002 and the implementation policy.

DOJ’s old good-faith enforcement-priority policy ran only through July 8, 2025 and is not continuing grace. Build a data/actor/access/agreement matrix and assign actual controls and reporting questions before access depends on approval. Keep personal data in authorised systems outside this site and assess other U.S., origin-country, sector, contractual and privacy obligations separately.

practicalOutput: A data/party/access/agreement matrix showing category counts, aggregation, transaction treatment, supported exemptions and unresolved technical duties.
limitations: No authorisation, exemption, security attestation or complete privacy clearance is supplied. CISA implementation details remain unresolved. The recorded October 5/October 6 difference is preserved; operative provisions control this explanation.

title: Is your U.S. licence also a franchise?
description: Look at the brand, operating support and required payments together before deciding how to sell the arrangement.
learningSummary: A licence gives another business permission to use specified rights, such as a name or trademark. If you also supply an operating system and require payment, U.S. franchise rules may apply even when the contract says “licence.” Start with what each business will actually do.

keyTerms.meaning: The business granting franchise rights; often the brand owner or its selling subsidiary.
The independent business receiving those rights and operating under the arrangement.
A name, logo or other sign identifying the commercial source of goods or services.
A rule that removes specified duties when its particular conditions are met; it does not necessarily change the relationship’s definition.

sections.heading: The business decision comes before the contract label
paragraphs: An established company may want local owners to find customers, employ staff and deliver its service under a common brand. Licensing sounds like a simple description of that plan. The legal question is broader: are you only allowing use of a protected name, or supplying a business method that the local owner will follow?

The U.S. Federal Trade Commission’s Franchise Rule examines a continuing commercial relationship involving trademark association, significant control or assistance over the operating method, and a required payment or commitment. Consider the three elements together. Describing the partner as an investor, distributor or licensee does not decide whether those facts are present.

sections.heading: Keep the definition and an exemption separate
paragraphs: First describe the relationship. Then examine whether a federal exclusion or exemption applies. An exemption has its own conditions; it is not a reason to omit inconvenient facts from the description. A federal conclusion also leaves independent state rules to examine. Different state definitions or sales requirements can produce additional work.

The useful management document is therefore a factual account, not a declaration that the model is “not a franchise.” Include the support promised in presentations and ordinary practice as well as the signed contract. Record payments to related companies too.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a maintenance brand builds a partner system
paragraphs: A European maintenance company proposes branded vans, a licence fee, mandatory scheduling software, initial training and required inspection methods. Its sales director initially treats these as separate purchases. Read together, however, they describe how the partner will operate the service.

The reviewer asks what the training covers, how much discretion the partner keeps, what the software controls and which payments are unavoidable. Software alone does not settle the test. Separating the licence, training and software charges into three invoices does not remove the need to examine them together. The next step is to establish the facts, not to announce a legal result.

sections.heading: Prepare one account of the relationship
paragraphs: Ask operations to describe delivery requirements, finance to map payments, and the expansion lead to identify the parties and locations. Keep unresolved answers visible.
bullets: List who signs customer contracts, employs staff and grants use of the brand.
Attach training outlines, software requirements, manuals and support promises.
Show each required payment or commitment, its recipient and timing, including related companies.
Record the planned outlet and the places from which offers are made or received.
Give the complete file to the person reviewing federal and relevant state requirements before relying on a classification.

practicalOutput: A relationship factsheet linking the actual rights, operating support, controls, payments and parties to the classification questions.
limitations: This guide explains the federal starting point; it does not classify a particular arrangement or decide an exemption. State and local requirements need their own analysis.

title: When does support become a franchise operating system?
description: Understand why training, software and service standards must be assessed together rather than counted as isolated features.
learningSummary: Brand owners often want independent operators to deliver a consistent service. The federal franchise inquiry asks whether the brand controls, or significantly assists, the operator’s overall way of running the business. The content and importance of the support matter more than the name of the document containing it.

keyTerms.meaning: The business supplying franchise rights and the associated brand or operating system.
The independent operator receiving those rights.
Support important to the operator’s overall method of doing business, assessed in the actual relationship.
Requirements protecting the brand owner’s rights in its name or mark; their purpose and extent matter.

sections.heading: Why ordinary support creates a legal question
paragraphs: A foreign brand may regard training and software as helpful extras. A new U.S. operator may rely on them to price jobs, allocate staff, win customers and deliver the service. That reliance helps explain why the federal inquiry considers the whole operating method rather than asking whether the contract includes a manual.

The definition addresses significant control or assistance. The brand’s right to impose controls matters as well as controls it has already exercised. Pre-contract promises and routine help also belong in the review; an incomplete contract summary can miss much of the actual system.

sections.heading: Distinguish protecting the name from directing the business
paragraphs: The FTC’s May 2008 Compliance Guide gives explanatory examples such as training, accounting systems, management advice and detailed manuals. It discusses the operator’s reasonable reliance and the overall method of operation. It is dated guidance, to be read with the current rule, not a current threshold sheet.

A requirement solely protecting legal ownership of a trademark differs from broader instructions about staffing, routes, sales methods or customer restrictions. Neither a logo guide nor a software subscription automatically decides the result. Ask what each requirement does in practice and how it connects to the rest of the system.

sections.heading: Fictional example: two different facilities-service documents
paragraphs: A facilities brand has a short logo guide specifying colours and approved use of its name. It also has a “quality appendix” covering which accounts operators accept, staffing levels, sales scripts, mandatory software, service reports and remedial visits.

The operations director explains each instruction’s purpose and supplies examples of support calls. The reviewer can then distinguish trademark protection from a wider operating system. Calling the second document an appendix does not reduce its importance. Equally, finding one detailed requirement is not a substitute for assessing the complete relationship.

sections.heading: Build a control-and-support inventory
paragraphs: For each requirement, record who can change it, whether it is mandatory in practice, how the brand monitors it and what happens if the operator ignores it. This inventory is a preparation tool, not a separate legal filing.
bullets: Collect manuals, software settings, training materials and sales promises.
Separate name/logo protection from requirements affecting business operations.
Identify promised help and the activities on which a new operator will reasonably depend.
Include contractual rights to intervene even where no intervention has yet happened.
Ask the reviewer to assess federal and relevant state tests before redesigning the commercial model.

practicalOutput: A practical inventory explaining the purpose, reach and use of every operating control and support commitment.
limitations: No individual manual, training course or software requirement automatically determines franchise status. The dated FTC guide supplies explanatory context; current federal law and independent state tests still govern.

title: The $735 federal exemption: which payments count?
description: Add required payments and commitments over the correct period; a delayed invoice or separate affiliate bill can still matter.
learningSummary: A low initial fee does not by itself settle U.S. franchise duties. The federal minimum-payment exemption uses a total of required payments and commitments, a defined time period, and a strict less-than comparison. Your finance team needs the whole payment arrangement before anyone relies on it.

keyTerms.meaning: The business granting the franchise rights.
A related company; required payments to it can matter as well as payments to the franchisor.
A payment or commitment required by contract or practical necessity, subject to the rule’s particular definition and exclusions.
The combined total, rather than each invoice considered separately.

sections.heading: Apply the current amount and time period
paragraphs: For this exemption, the total required payments or commitments to the franchisor or an affiliate must be less than $735, counting from before operations begin through six months after they commence. Exactly $735 is not less than $735. These are the amount and period in 16 CFR 436.8(a)(1).

This is an exemption from specified federal franchise disclosure requirements, not the universal definition of a franchise and not an exemption from state law. Assess the relationship’s brand, operating-control or assistance, and payment facts before treating the payment exemption as the answer to the entire legal question. Older material quoting $500 does not supply the current amount.

sections.heading: Read the commitment as well as the bank statement
paragraphs: Include required training, software, equipment, royalties and purchases from related companies where the rule’s payment definition reaches them. A fee can matter even before cash changes hands if the partner has made the relevant commitment to pay.

The required-payment definition has a specific exclusion for reasonable quantities of inventory bought at bona fide wholesale prices for resale or lease. It does not remove every supply purchase. A service company should not assume that equipment or materials used to deliver its service automatically fall within an inventory-for-resale exclusion.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a fee split into three parts
paragraphs: A brand proposes a $300 initial fee and requires a $250 training payment and a $250 software commitment to its affiliate within the relevant period. Assuming all three are required payments within the rule, the total is $800. Looking only at the $300 initial invoice would miss the relevant total.

The brand then suggests collecting the software money later. Finance still needs to show when the obligation is undertaken, not merely the proposed collection date. The reviewer must decide the actual treatment from the agreement and business facts; this illustration does not establish an exemption for a real transaction.

sections.heading: Produce a payment schedule that can be checked
paragraphs: Use the actual proposed start date and list each payment alongside the commitment date, due date, recipient, purpose and reason it is required. Mark an unknown amount as unknown rather than zero.
bullets: Reconcile the main agreement, training terms, software orders and affiliate purchases.
Identify any claimed inventory exclusion and the facts supporting it.
Ask the reviewer to apply the precise period and less-than-$735 comparison.
Keep separate questions for relevant state franchise, business-opportunity, dealer, advertising and relationship rules.

practicalOutput: A dated schedule of all required payments and commitments, with any claimed exclusions and separate state questions.
limitations: The $735 figure and six-month period belong to this specific federal exemption. They do not decide state treatment or approve a payment structure.

title: Does one trademark licence avoid franchise disclosure?
description: A narrow single-license treatment concerns the complete licensing arrangement, not one agreement in each state.
learningSummary: A brand planning its first U.S. partner may hear that “one licence is exempt.” That shorthand can be misleading. The federal guidance discusses a narrow single-trademark-license situation, and the number of licensees is different from the number of outlets they operate.

keyTerms.meaning: The person or business receiving permission to use the trademark.
An operating location; one licensee can have more than one outlet.
Treatment placing a stated arrangement outside the rule as explained in the relevant authority.
An agency staff view on represented facts, which may be nonbinding rather than a Commission ruling.

sections.heading: Start with the complete licensing plan
paragraphs: The FTC Compliance Guide describes a narrow exclusion for a single licensee using a trademark. That description is not one free franchise, one free outlet, or one licence in every state. A brand’s existing grants and intended later grants therefore matter.

Do not isolate the first signed contract from the planned network. The reviewer needs to know what rights have been granted, who holds them and what the brand expects to grant next. Separate state rules remain a question even if the narrow federal treatment is available.

sections.heading: Understand what the historical opinion can establish
paragraphs: FTC staff opinion 05-1, dated January 5, 2005, addressed a particular salon arrangement using an earlier rule citation. Staff expressly said that its view was not binding on the Commission. Its discussion distinguishes licensees from outlets and notes that intended future licences would change the analysis.

The opinion helps identify relevant questions. It does not give today’s applicant a ruling simply because its proposal also involves a salon or one initial contract. The May 2008 guide is explanatory material too; the historical dates and limited authority should remain clear when using it.

sections.heading: Fictional example: “exclusive” rights in three states
paragraphs: A European service brand proposes a Texas licence for Company A, a California licence for Company B and an Illinois licence for Company C. Each agreement says the local company is the sole licensee in its state. There are nevertheless three proposed licensees in the overall plan. State-by-state exclusivity does not turn that plan into a single-license arrangement.

Conversely, counting buildings alone can be misleading where a single licensee runs several outlets. That distinction is a reason to obtain a complete factual review, not a conclusion that any multi-outlet arrangement qualifies.

sections.heading: Prepare a grant register before relying on the shorthand
paragraphs: The expansion lead should collect current and intended rights in one register. Include the actual legal entities rather than just trading names.
bullets: Identify each mark, licensed goods or services, licensee and affiliate involved.
Separate the number of licensees from their operating locations.
Attach existing agreements, planned grants and termination rights.
Explain the intended rollout, including future independent operators.
Ask whether the exact federal treatment and any comparable state treatment are available on those facts.

practicalOutput: A complete trademark-grant register and a precise question about the narrow single-license treatment.
limitations: The historical staff opinion is fact-specific and nonbinding. This guide does not decide eligibility, future-license effects or independent state requirements.

title: Which U.S. places matter when recruiting a partner?
description: Map the seller, buyer, proposed business and communications before choosing the states to review.
learningSummary: A brand may think only the future outlet’s state matters. Franchise sales rules can also depend on the parties and where an offer starts or is received. A simple transaction map gives the reviewer the facts needed to decide which state requirements reach the proposed activity.

keyTerms.meaning: The business offering franchise rights, which may be a subsidiary rather than the foreign parent.
The person or business considering the purchase.
A sales communication or proposal whose legal treatment depends on the applicable law and actual content.
A fact linking the activity to a state, sometimes called nexus; its legal importance depends on the particular rule.

sections.heading: Why one outlet address is not enough
paragraphs: Federal disclosure and state franchise-sales rules are separate layers. The federal rule preserves state and local franchise-practices laws except to the extent of inconsistency; equal or greater protection is not inconsistent. A federal disclosure process therefore does not replace the state analysis.

The relevant state questions can involve the seller’s location, the buyer’s residence, the operating location, and where communications originate or are received. This guide identifies facts to collect. It does not assert that every one of those connections triggers every state law.

sections.heading: Describe what happens before the final agreement
paragraphs: A recruitment process may include website advertising, broker introductions, discovery meetings, territory discussions, disclosure, deposits and signing. Those steps should not be reduced to a single proposed opening date. What the communication contains, where the people are, and whether money or a binding promise arises can change the review.

There is no universal prohibition on introductory calls stated here. The useful question is what this particular call or document proposes and which applicable law governs it. Similarly, an internal spreadsheet saying “registration complete” should identify the actual state, entity, offering and evidence.

sections.heading: Fictional example: New York buyer, Florida operation
paragraphs: A Singapore parent speaks with a prospective partner who lives in New York about a Florida operation. A U.S. subsidiary will sell the rights, and a broker introduces the parties. A worksheet containing only “Florida outlet” leaves important facts out.

The expansion lead adds each entity’s identity, each participant’s location, the proposed communications, the intended contracting party and any deposit. The reviewer can then examine the relevant state connections and exemptions. The example does not decide that a particular New York or Florida filing is required; it shows why a fuller map is needed before that decision.

sections.heading: Use separate columns for separate duties
paragraphs: Create a table with a row for each potentially relevant jurisdiction. Keep classification, registration, notice, exemption, disclosure, advertising and continuing relationship rules in separate columns. These terms ask different questions: whether the model is covered, whether a filing is needed, what information must be given, and how the relationship is regulated.

Assign a named person and supporting document to each conclusion. A blank means unresearched, not no requirement. Retain the facts and reasoning supporting any conclusion that a rule does not apply. Operational permits and other local business obligations belong in additional checks.

practicalOutput: A transaction map showing seller, buyer, proposed outlet and communication locations, linked to separate jurisdictional questions.
limitations: No particular state’s reach, exemption or filing requirement is determined here. Federal sales disclosure and operating permissions remain separate layers.

title: When must a prospective partner receive the FDD?
description: Plan disclosure around the first relevant agreement or payment, including an earlier territory deposit.
learningSummary: An FDD, or Franchise Disclosure Document, gives a prospective franchisee information about the offering before committing. For a covered sale, delivering it is the franchisor’s responsibility. The waiting period must be planned around the earliest relevant agreement or payment, not just the ceremonial signing date.

keyTerms.meaning: The business granting the franchise rights and responsible for furnishing the disclosure document.
The person or business considering buying those rights.
The required disclosure document describing the franchise offering; it is not government approval or a profit promise.
Days counted on the calendar, rather than only working days; apply the rule’s actual counting and delivery requirements.

sections.heading: Understand the federal waiting period
paragraphs: For a covered, nonexempt franchise to be located in the United States or its territories, the current FDD generally must be furnished at least 14 calendar days before the prospective franchisee signs a binding agreement with, or makes payment to, the franchisor or an affiliate in connection with the proposed sale. An affiliate is a related company.

Both agreement and payment matter. Moving a charge to a related company does not by itself remove the payment question. Nor should the team assume that money falls outside the review merely because it is called a reservation or can be refunded.

sections.heading: Find the first commitment in the actual sales process
paragraphs: Work backwards from every proposed binding document or payment, not only the final franchise agreement. A territory reservation, preliminary agreement or deposit may occur earlier. Record what each document actually commits the parties to and why each payment is requested.

Keep the document version and exhibits furnished to this prospect. Section 436.2 specifies delivery methods, including particular treatment for mailing. Choose a permitted method and have the counting and delivery evidence checked. An educational website visit or a tick beside a training module is not evidence that the required FDD was furnished.

sections.heading: Fictional example: the deposit comes first
paragraphs: A Dutch industrial-services brand expects to sign a franchise agreement near the end of a month. Its sales manager asks the candidate to pay a territory deposit earlier so another applicant cannot take the area. The manager has calculated the disclosure timetable only from the final signing date.

The disclosure coordinator adds the deposit request to the timetable and sends its terms for review. If it is a relevant payment, the waiting period must be satisfied before that earlier event. Postponing the final signature would not cure a premature payment. The team checks state requirements and any later agreement changes separately; this example does not decide the treatment of a particular reservation.

sections.heading: Maintain a prospect-specific disclosure log
paragraphs: The log is an internal control supporting the legal delivery obligation. A named person should check the earliest agreement/payment date before sales staff ask for either.
bullets: Identify the actual recipient and the franchisor or related payee.
Store the current FDD and all proposed agreements actually furnished.
Record method, date and evidence of delivery, plus any receipt.
Record updates and revised agreements without overwriting the earlier files.
Check the applicable federal period, method and independent state requirements before releasing signing or payment requests.

practicalOutput: A prospect-specific disclosure log connecting the delivered documents, evidence of delivery and earliest proposed agreement or payment.
limitations: Federal timing is only one layer. Exemptions, delivery/counting details, state rules and later document changes require their own assessment. A receipt records delivery; it does not approve the offering or waive rights.

title: What changes when the franchise agreement is revised?
description: Distinguish a material change imposed by the franchisor from a change arising from negotiations started by the prospect.
learningSummary: Negotiations often continue after the FDD has been delivered. A new charge or obligation can change what the prospective franchisee is being asked to accept. The federal rule gives certain revised agreements a separate waiting period, so the sales team needs a record of what changed and who initiated it.

keyTerms.meaning: The business granting the rights and proposing the franchise agreement.
A change important enough to require the legal assessment discussed here; not every drafting edit is automatically material.
A change made on the franchisor’s initiative, rather than arising from negotiations initiated by the prospect.
An additional agreement attached to the FDD as part of the proposed arrangement.

sections.heading: The seven-day requirement has a particular trigger
paragraphs: A franchisor that unilaterally and materially changes the attached basic franchise agreement or related agreements must furnish each revised agreement at least seven calendar days before it is signed. This revised-agreement requirement sits alongside the general FDD disclosure period (16 CFR 436.2(b)).

It is not a rule that every edit restarts every clock. First establish whether the change is material, whether it is unilateral and which agreement has changed. The exact revised documents and proposed signature date matter.

sections.heading: Keep prospect-initiated negotiations distinguishable
paragraphs: The text treats changes arising from negotiations initiated by the prospective franchisee differently: those changes do not trigger this particular seven-day period. That distinction requires facts. Calling a change “negotiated” in the file is not enough if the franchisor proposed it.

Record the request, the earlier wording, the proposed wording and its commercial effect. Keep emails or meeting notes showing who raised the issue. A clean final agreement helps signing, but a marked comparison helps the reviewer understand whether the timing rule applies. State amendment or further-disclosure requirements remain separate.

sections.heading: Fictional example: two changes with different histories
paragraphs: After providing its FDD, a brand decides all new operators must pay a new field-support charge. The prospect did not request it. The team preserves the old and new provisions and asks whether this is a unilateral material change requiring revised-agreement delivery and the seven-calendar-day period. An informal sales assurance cannot answer that question.

In the same transaction, the prospect asks to alter a territory boundary during negotiations. That change has a different origin. The file should show the request and negotiations rather than combine both changes under one label. Neither example supplies a universal materiality ruling or decides state-law requirements.

sections.heading: Give legal, sales and operations distinct jobs
paragraphs: The reviewer determines the legal effect and timing. Sales prevents premature signatures and payment requests under the applicable process. Operations confirms whether revised support promises can actually be performed.
bullets: Maintain a dated change log for every basic or related agreement.
Identify the initiating party and retain the request or decision.
Save delivered revisions with the prospect’s earlier FDD record.
Check the seven-day trigger, general disclosure timing and relevant state requirements separately.
Communicate the reviewed signing date to everyone handling the transaction.

practicalOutput: A dated agreement-change record showing who initiated each revision, its effect, delivery and reviewed signing timetable.
limitations: Not every edit is material, and prospect-initiated negotiations have distinct federal treatment. This guide does not determine a particular change or any independent state amendment or disclosure duty.

title: Keeping the FDD current as the business changes
description: Give finance, operations and development a shared process for annual updates, material changes and retained versions.
learningSummary: An FDD describes a business that continues to change after the document is first prepared. The franchisor needs a process for collecting changes, updating disclosure and knowing which version each prospect received. Treating the FDD as an annual marketing-design project leaves important responsibilities unassigned.

keyTerms.meaning: The business selling the franchise rights and maintaining its disclosure document.
The company’s financial reporting year, which need not end on December 31.
An important change requiring assessment under the applicable disclosure rules.
The FDD item addressing financial performance representations, such as specified sales or profit claims.

sections.heading: Use separate annual and quarterly clocks
paragraphs: The federal rule requires a revised FDD within 120 days after the end of the fiscal year, followed by distribution of only the revised document. It also calls for quarterly revisions within a reasonable time after quarter-end for material changes. Do not convert “reasonable time” into an invented fixed number of days.

Known material changes in Item 19 information must be communicated when the FDD is furnished. That specific requirement needs its own check; waiting for the next annual revision is not a complete approach to changing performance information. State renewals and amendments also need separate calendars.

sections.heading: Collect changes from the people who know them
paragraphs: Finance holds statements, fee information and financial-performance data. Operations knows about training, suppliers, personnel and support arrangements. Development maintains outlet information. The person managing disputes and agreements knows about changes that other teams may not see.

Create a simple intake record stating what happened, when, which disclosure it may affect and who will assess it. A team member reports the business fact; the responsible reviewer decides the disclosure consequence. Keep those roles distinct rather than expecting every manager to make a legal materiality decision.

sections.heading: Fictional example: support is outsourced mid-year
paragraphs: A French service brand transfers U.S. field support to a contractor after delivering its annual FDD. The operations lead records the new provider, changed personnel, service commitments and relevant contractual wording. The disclosure owner compares those facts with what prospects have been told.

The issue is not whether the next brochure looks outdated. It is whether assistance or other required information has materially changed, which updates or communications are needed, and which prospects received an earlier version. The team records that assessment while continuing to maintain its separate state filing calendar.

sections.heading: Keep old versions and completed-sale receipts
paragraphs: The federal rule requires materially different FDD versions to be kept for three years after the close of the fiscal year in which each was last used (§ 436.6(h)). Signed receipts for completed sales must be kept for at least three years (§ 436.6(i)). These are different retention descriptions.

Use a controlled repository with a named owner. Preserve the actual files furnished, their use dates and the matching prospect records. Replacing an old file with an edited document of the same name destroys the ability to explain what was disclosed at the time.

practicalOutput: An update calendar and change register linked to controlled FDD versions, prospect delivery records and retained completed-sale receipts.
limitations: This guide explains the named federal update and record duties. State renewal/amendment requirements and whether a particular event is material remain separate questions.

title: Can home-market sales figures be used to recruit U.S. partners?
description: Understand when a revenue example becomes an earnings claim and what evidence must support it.
learningSummary: Owners often explain an expansion opportunity by showing how their existing outlets perform. Once those figures reach prospective franchisees, they can become regulated financial performance representations. A credible home-market result is not automatically a lawful U.S. sales claim or evidence of a U.S. operator’s profit.

keyTerms.meaning: A statement about specified actual or potential sales, income, gross profit or net profit, including a mathematical calculation.
The FDD section for the required treatment of financial performance representations.
Documents and data supporting the claim, rather than a salesperson’s assurance.
Revenue is sales income; profit depends on the relevant costs and calculation, so the figures are not interchangeable.

sections.heading: A claim can appear in a spreadsheet or conversation
paragraphs: The federal definition reaches oral, written and visual statements and mathematical calculations. A slide, calculator result, message or spoken answer can therefore matter as well as a formal forecast. Calling a figure illustrative does not itself decide its legal treatment.

An internal planning model has a different audience from a recruitment presentation. Before sending it to prospects, examine what it represents and whether the required basis, supporting documents and disclosure conditions are satisfied. The franchisor should also control what brokers and other sellers say.

sections.heading: Answer Item 19 even when choosing not to make a claim
paragraphs: A franchisor may elect not to make a financial performance representation, but it must still answer Item 19 with the required negative disclosure. Where a representation is made, a reasonable basis, written substantiation and the item’s requirements matter.

There is defined treatment for specific-outlet records and compliant supplemental representations. Those are conditional routes, not permission to give any figures privately. Have the exact proposed statement and supporting material reviewed before relying on an exception or supplement.

sections.heading: Fictional example: $1 million of Singapore cleaning revenue
paragraphs: A Singapore cleaning outlet reports annual revenue equivalent to US$1 million. The brand wants to put that figure beside a U.S. territory map. Finance can verify the currency conversion, but that does not establish what a U.S. operator will sell or retain as profit.

The reader needs to understand the operating period, customer mix, included outlets and whether costs are omitted. U.S. management pay, insurance, collections and local sales costs may differ. Selecting one strong outlet may also give a misleading picture of the wider group. The reviewer therefore examines the proposed claim, relevant data and material differences, rather than approving a headline because its arithmetic is correct.

sections.heading: Prepare a claim file before approving sales materials
paragraphs: The following is a practical preparation list supporting the applicable legal requirements, not an extra filing by itself.
bullets: Write the exact claim, audience and communication channel.
Identify source entities, period, currency and conversion method.
Explain which outlets are included or excluded, sample size and distribution of results.
Identify omitted costs and differences between the source operation and proposed U.S. business.
Keep written supporting material and the reviewed Item 19 treatment with the approved version.
Route new calculations and salesperson variations back through the same review.

practicalOutput: A claim-by-claim file connecting proposed wording, source data, limitations, written support and the applicable Item 19 treatment.
limitations: No home-market result or projection is approved here. Specific-outlet and supplemental routes have their own conditions; independent state requirements remain separate.

title: Area developer or master partner: who runs and supports the units?
description: Compare the actual contracts, sales duties and support work before giving a partner a regional title.
learningSummary: A strong branch manager may be able to open more company-operated units without being ready to recruit and support independent owners. Area development and master arrangements can therefore require very different capabilities. Draw the jobs and payment flows before choosing a title.

keyTerms.meaning: An operator typically undertaking to develop its own units over time under agreed rights.
An arrangement that can authorise granting subfranchises and supporting independent operators; the actual rights matter.
An intermediary covered by the federal franchisor definition when it engages in both pre-sale activities and post-sale performance.
A party that may help recruit or support operators while the brand remains their contracting franchisor.

sections.heading: Separate delivering services from supporting business owners
paragraphs: An own-unit operator recruits staff, wins customers and delivers the service through its business. An area developer adds an agreed development programme for its own units. A master arrangement can add independent-owner recruitment, disclosure, contracting, training, support and disputes. Those are additional jobs, not simply a larger sales territory.

Titles vary. Distribution and intellectual-property licensing also require their own analysis of goods, payments and controls. A contract heading cannot establish who performs the work or which legal rules apply.

sections.heading: Why the intermediary’s role matters legally
paragraphs: An intermediary can fall within the federal franchisor definition as a subfranchisor when it engages in both pre-sale activities and post-sale performance (§ 436.1(k)). Identify the actual conduct rather than assuming only the foreign brand has responsibilities. Item 21 also specifies separate subfranchisor financial statements in the relevant arrangement.

A role allocation helps explain who does what, but does not erase regulatory duties. Keep three diagrams if necessary: who contracts with whom, where the money goes, and who provides operating support. They may show different relationships.

sections.heading: Fictional example: four managed branches are not yet a network
paragraphs: A French industrial-maintenance operator successfully manages four branches. It proposes recruiting independent U.S. owners under a master agreement. Its existing evidence shows that it can train employees and serve customers, but it has no franchise-sales process or dedicated owner-support team.

The brand compares two plans. An own-unit development plan builds on current delivery capability. A subfranchise plan requires additional people, sales controls, disclosure records and ongoing support funding. This is a commercial capability comparison, not a recommendation that one legal structure is available or preferable for the actual parties.

sections.heading: Test the recurring costs, not just the first territory fee
paragraphs: Use a responsibility table and ask for evidence behind each proposed role. As optional business planning, model a slower rollout and a period without new upfront fees. Continuing obligations still need funding when recruitment is delayed.

rows: Managers, customer contracts, quality records and financial information
Trained sales staff, lawful materials, disclosure process and records
Support headcount, training/visit budget, systems and escalation process

sections.heading: Turn the comparison into an accountable plan
paragraphs: Identify every contracting and fee-receiving entity. Allocate recruitment, approvals, disclosure, fees, training, bid support, quality monitoring and disputes. Separate tasks performed for own units from tasks owed to independent operators. Then ask the reviewer to assess the relevant federal and state definitions, disclosure, financial-statement and exemption questions.

practicalOutput: A role, contract, payment and support diagram with evidence of capability and a recurring-cost budget for each participant.
limitations: The model descriptions are practical comparisons, not universal legal definitions. Actual conduct, financial-disclosure requirements and state treatment require separate review.

title: Will your existing foreign audit work for the U.S. FDD?
description: Identify the right companies, accounting basis and audit standards before promising a launch date.
learningSummary: An established foreign business may already publish audited accounts. That is useful evidence, but it does not automatically satisfy the U.S. franchise disclosure requirements. The selling entity, supporting parent and any subfranchisor can affect which statements are needed.

keyTerms.meaning: The FDD item specifying financial statements and audit requirements.
The rules used to prepare the financial statements, such as U.S. GAAP or another permitted basis.
The standards governing the auditor’s examination; these are distinct from the preparation basis.
The companies whose statements must be included, determined from the applicable rule and actual arrangement.

sections.heading: Treat preparation and audit as two questions
paragraphs: Item 21 specifies financial statements prepared under U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, commonly called U.S. GAAP, or principles permitted by the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the applicable U.S. generally accepted auditing standards. Having an audit does not by itself answer either question.

The FTC’s May 2008 explanatory guide discusses foreign accounting, but its age matters. The responsible auditor should confirm current SEC-permitted treatment rather than reading that guide as blanket acceptance of any accounts prepared under International Financial Reporting Standards. Identify the proposed basis and audit approach expressly.

sections.heading: Map the promises before choosing the accounts
paragraphs: The company selling U.S. franchise rights may be a new subsidiary rather than the foreign parent. The group may nevertheless promise that the parent will train operators, provide support or guarantee obligations. Subfranchisor roles can add further financial-disclosure questions.

Give the reviewer the actual agreements and guarantees, not only an organisation chart. A thin selling subsidiary does not make the parent’s promises disappear. Conversely, the existence of a strong parent does not automatically permit the subsidiary simply to attach the parent’s annual report.

sections.heading: Fictional example: the parent supplies the support
paragraphs: A European group forms a U.S. company to sell franchises. Its presentations say the European parent will train every new operator and provide technical support. Finance initially budgets only for the subsidiary’s opening accounts.

The CFO collects the support wording, any guarantees and the proposed contracts. The reviewer and auditor identify the relevant entities, reporting dates, preparation basis and audit work. If reconciliation or additional statements are needed, that affects the timetable. The example identifies a preparation gap; it does not decide the exact statements required for that group.

sections.heading: Commission a written scope before sales promise a date
paragraphs: Ask the auditor for a work plan stating which entities and periods are covered, the accounting and audit standards, any reconciliation approach and the expected delivery date. Coordinate that plan with the actual disclosure schedule.

The federal startup phase-in has conditions. It is not a universal shortcut for an established foreign system and does not establish acceptance under state rules. Financial-assurance questions also need their own review. Keep those unresolved issues visible in the launch budget and calendar rather than treating them as completed because an audit engagement has been signed.

practicalOutput: A written auditor/reviewer scope identifying required entities, reporting periods, preparation basis, audit standards, timetable and unresolved acceptance questions.
limitations: This guide does not approve particular foreign accounts, SEC treatment or startup eligibility. State acceptance and financial-assurance conditions remain separate questions.

title: How much of a U.S. royalty reaches the foreign brand?
description: Separate the contract amount, tax withheld and cash received before budgeting overseas support.
learningSummary: A U.S. operator may promise a royalty to the overseas brand, but the invoice amount may differ from the cash the brand receives. The payer may have withholding and reporting responsibilities. Build the cash model only after identifying the payment, recipient and applicable tax treatment.

keyTerms.meaning: A payment for the relevant rights, such as use of a brand; its actual tax character must be assessed.
Tax the payer deducts and remits instead of sending that amount to the recipient.
The person or entity entitled to the income for the relevant tax analysis, which is not answered merely by a mailing address.
Contract wording that may increase the payer’s cost so the recipient receives a specified amount after withholding.

sections.heading: Start with the payment and recipient
paragraphs: The Internal Revenue Service describes a general 30% withholding regime for many types of U.S.-source income paid to foreign persons. Statutory or treaty relief may reduce the result, depending on the facts and documentation. This is not a statement that every cross-border payment bears 30%.

Ask first what the payment is for, where the relevant income is sourced, who receives and beneficially owns it, and whether the claimed relief applies. Incorporation in a treaty country or a company address is not a complete treaty analysis. Applicable conditions and limitation provisions need their own review.

sections.heading: Show three cash lines instead of one royalty headline
paragraphs: The budget should display the contractual gross royalty, the amount withheld and remitted, and the cash received by the foreign brand. If the agreement contains a gross-up, model its effect on the payer’s cost rather than assuming the written royalty is the whole expense.

This is useful business planning alongside the tax analysis. The applicable rate stays an assumption until reviewed. An unknown rate should not silently become zero in a forecast, particularly when the brand is relying on royalty receipts to fund training and support.

sections.heading: Fictional example: sensitivity, not a treaty quotation
paragraphs: Assume an annual gross royalty of US$100,000 and a hypothetical 10% withholding rate solely to examine cash sensitivity. The payer withholds US$10,000, leaving US$90,000 for the foreign brand before support costs. The example does not identify an actual treaty rate for any country.

If the commercial plan had allocated the full US$100,000 to overseas support, it would now have a funding gap. Finance must resolve the actual rate, documentation and any gross-up terms before treating the support budget as funded. Correct arithmetic cannot establish entitlement to treaty relief.

sections.heading: Give the reporting job a named owner
paragraphs: Forms 1042 and 1042-S belong to the withholding/reporting process. A reduced withholding rate does not itself prove there is no reporting duty. The CFO should agree responsibilities with the relevant preparer and payer before the first covered payment.
bullets: Identify the contracting payer, payee and beneficial owner.
Describe the payment and the proposed sourcing treatment.
Document treaty/statutory conditions and appropriate withholding certificates.
Record who deducts, deposits, files and supplies reporting documents.
Reconcile gross, withheld and net cash with the support budget and agreement.

practicalOutput: A gross-to-net royalty schedule and a named payer/preparer responsibility list for documentation, withholding and reporting.
limitations: No actual country rate, treaty entitlement, source classification or filing outcome is determined here. The 10% illustration is arithmetic only.

title: Does this company fall within the current FinCEN reporting rule?
description: Distinguish a company created in the United States from a foreign company registered to do business there.
learningSummary: A company can be foreign-owned without having been formed abroad. That distinction is central to the narrowed beneficial-ownership reporting rule recorded in this review. Identify the actual legal entity and its formation and registration events before using an old onboarding checklist.

keyTerms.meaning: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, the U.S. agency administering the reporting rule discussed here.
Beneficial ownership information: the information covered by the relevant reporting requirements.
For this distinction, a company created in the United States, even if its owners are foreign.
A filing registering an already foreign-formed entity to do business in a U.S. state or tribal jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Foreign ownership and foreign formation ask different questions
paragraphs: As recorded in the November 12, 2026 review,31 CFR 1010.380 exempts U.S.-created domestic entities. A nonexempt entity formed abroad and registered by filing in a U.S. state or tribal jurisdiction can remain a reporting company. The owners’ nationality alone does not answer which branch applies.

Read the entity’s formation record and the actual registration filing. A group may contain both a U.S.-created subsidiary and a foreign parent registered separately. A conclusion about one company is not automatically a conclusion about every company in the group.

sections.heading: Use the narrowed rule and the relevant notice date
paragraphs: FinCEN’s final rule effective August 14, 2026 preserves the narrowed scope and provides specified relief for U.S.-person beneficial-owner and company-applicant information. Older 2024 or early-2025 checklists can describe superseded duties. Do not ask for documents merely because a historic checklist includes them.

For new in-scope reporting companies on or after March 26, 2025, the recorded rule uses 30 calendar days from the earlier actual or public registration notice, subject to applicable relief. Identify both possible notice events rather than starting from an informal internal announcement. Check current exemptions and any applicable judicial or agency relief at the filing date.

sections.heading: Fictional example: two Malaysian expansion structures
paragraphs: In one plan, a Malaysian company creates a new U.S. subsidiary. In another, it registers the Malaysian entity itself to do business in a state. The first plan involves a U.S.-created entity; the second involves a foreign-formed entity and a U.S. registration event.

The company secretary records those differences and asks whether the foreign registration is in scope or covered by another exemption. The subsidiary’s domestic exemption does not decide a separate parent registration. Neither example determines the actual company’s complete reporting or tax position.

sections.heading: Keep a safe status record
paragraphs: For planning, record the formation jurisdiction, registration event, relevant dates, exemption analysis and responsible filer. Store only non-sensitive task status in this educational process. Do not upload passports or identity documents.

Keep Internal Revenue Service (IRS) reporting, state annual reports, banking and sanctions checks separate. “Exempt from this BOI rule” is a specific conclusion about one reporting regime, not permission to omit unrelated company obligations.

practicalOutput: An entity-by-entity BOI scope record showing formation, registration, notice dates, applicable exemption/relief and responsible filer.
